name: Mazatlán Ceviche de Sierra (Sinaloan Mackerel Ceviche)

ingredients.name: fresh lime juice, from about 6 whole Persian limes
loosely packed finely chopped fresh cilantro leaves, tender stems

instructions.primary_message: Using a very sharp knife, cut the fish into 1.5-cm cubes. Transfer to a large plate or baking sheet in a single layer and freeze until the fish is firm to the touch but not fully frozen, about 30 minutes. Meanwhile, place a food processor bowl and its blade into the freezer to chill while the fish is freezing.
Toss carrot with 1/4 teaspoon salt and transfer to a fine-mesh strainer set over a bowl. Let drain for 20 minutes, gently pressing on the carrots to remove excess moisture.

Once the fish is firm, transfer to the food processor and pulse until evenly ground, about 10 to 20 pulses (fish should be roughly 0.5 cm in size; be careful not to over-process fish to a smooth paste).

Transfer fish to a mixing bowl and toss well with onion, lime juice, remaining 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, and pepper to taste. Let marinate in refrigerator, stirring occasionally, until the fish turns from translucent to opaque white, 5 to 10 minutes.
Stir in the drained grated carrot and cilantro. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Top with cucumber and serve right away with tostadas, mayonnaise, avocado, and sauces.

description: This tart, refreshing, and slightly sweet fresh fish ceviche is perfect for lunch on a hot day.
notes:
Optional or for serving: Salsa negra or hot sauce of your choice (common options include a fresh serrano salsa, Valentina or Salsa Huichol)

Optional substitutions: sushi-grade skinless Pacific sierra → mahi fillets

Notes: This recipe is traditionally made with Pacific sierra, a fish in the mackerel family. If unavailable, mahi mahi may be substituted, as can Spanish mackerel. Mahi mahi is less assertive in flavor and slightly sweeter than Pacific sierra, while Spanish mackerel is an oilier and more flavorful fish. Make sure to buy extremely fresh fish that is suitable for eating raw; flash-frozen fish is even safer, as the deep-freezing process kills some potential parasites.
This recipe traditionally uses ground fish. While a food processor does a good job "grinding" the fish and is easy to use, you can also finely chop the fish with a very sharp knife to 0.5-cm pieces.
Key limes are common in Mexico and will also work in this recipe; I recommend using good quality key limes if you can find them. They should be plump, green, and heavy, and about 4 cm in diameter; you will need more key limes than Persian limes, if you use them.

Make-ahead and storage: This recipe is best prepared fresh right before serving. Ceviche should otherwise be kept refrigerated and eaten the same day it is prepared.
author: Rose Egelhoff
